articles.description: Germany: Half Of All People Convicted In Bavaria Was A Foreigner Last Year Via Remix News , Foreigners make up an incredible share of the people convicted of a crime in the German state of Bavaria, considered one of the wealthiest regions in Europe. The latest figures show that 49.7 percent of all people convicted of a crime in 2025 were foreigners, representing 52,679 people , according to data released by Bavarian Justice Minister Josef Schmid (CSU). The data shows that 105,938 people were convicted by final judgment, representing a 4.3 percent decline from the previous year. However, even as crime declines, foreigners account for a higher and higher share of convictions . That share has risen from 34.3 percent in 2015 and edged up to 49.3 percent in 2024, even as the absolute number of non-German convictions fell by 3.4 percent. Foreign nationals make up roughly 15.6 percent of Bavaria's population, which totals 2.07 million of 13.25 million residents. As a result, their share among the convicted is more than three times their population number . articles.description: A new book, With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna, reveals the deep-rooted queer subcultures in cities from Budapest to Prague – defying regional stereotypes and inspiring an art exhibition on masculinity The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein argued that our understanding of reality is fundamentally bound by and shaped by the language we use to talk about it. But there is one place where the Vienna-born thinker’s argument ceases to make sense. “Gay saunas are spaces where language dies,” says Vratislav Maňák, a Czech writer and literary scholar. With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna, a book that made a major splash when it was published in Czech and German earlier this year, Maňák fictionalises Wittgenstein, who had romantic relations with both men and women , entering a Viennese Herrensauna called Kaiserbründl, hailed in newspapers at the time as “the most stylish bathing establishment in the world”. Continue reading...

articles.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
articles.description: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
articles.description: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?
articles.description: When our writer found himself among the hundreds on Oxford Street hoping to get their hands on early copies and collectibles, it was a heartwarming reminder of the shared experience of fandom • The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true It is Thursday night and I am sat blurry-eyed and runny nosed outside the Argos on Oxford Street. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills. These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. But in a bygone era, when we used to go to shops to buy games, midnight launches offered a space for likeminded enthusiasts to gather and celebrate their fandom. Every Call

articles.title: Caryl Churchill’s magnificent Cloud 9 reaches for the skies – the National Theatre has done it proud
articles.description: National Theatre, London The experimental 1979 drama gleefully muddles roles in a century-spanning caper that bounces from colonial Africa to hippy London Caryl Churchill’s time-hopping 1979 drama is not revived as often as it might be, perhaps because it is so magnificently madcap. Bouncing from a first act satirising Victorian life in colonial Africa to a second act exploring sexual liberation in 1970s London, it could easily roll off-kilter in the wrong hands. There is also its complicated framework. Cloud 9 is a play in two distinct parts which follows some of the characters a century on, although they only age 25 years in that time and are played by different actors through ironic cross-casting. Thankfully this crisp, handsome and note-perfect revival lands in exactly the right hands with director Dominic Cooke, clear as crystal despite the complications, sizzling with satire but showing itself to be a deadly serious, and still highly topical, play about identity beneath its playful sending up of everything from empire and Britishness to the confinements of marriage. Continue reading...

articles.title: Old Vic 2027 season to feature Damian Lewis in a ‘provocative’ Henry V and Milly Alcock as Miss Julie
articles.description: Rupert Goold begins his tenure as artistic director with a version of Shakespeare’s history play, followed by shows starring Supergirl’s Alcock and Arinzé Kene Damian Lewis is to play Henry V at the Old Vic in London in the first production under the theatre’s new artistic director, Rupert Goold. Goold will direct what is billed as a “provocative” version of Shakespeare’s history play that challenges “what makes a leader a legend”. It will be Lewis’s first major theatre role since he starred in The Goat, or Who Is Sylvia? almost 10 years ago. He has previously played Romeo and Hamlet on stage, as well as appearing in Cymbeline and Much Ado About Nothing for the Royal Shakespeare Company. Continue reading...

articles.title: There’s scurvy, mutiny and mystery in Dogstar – but like its icebound ship this drama goes nowhere
articles.description: Hampstead theatre, London A bickering trio of trapped survivors who have lost their comrades are kept in an ominous stasis in Daisy Bell’s play The setup is strong in Daisy Hall’s follow-up to her debut, Bellringers . A few survivors on a whaling ship trapped in arctic ice are figuring out how to break free as the ice groans and explodes ominously around them. Babben (Justin Edwards) is an old hand who has whaled for almost 40 years; Gorey (Adam Rojko Vega) is a mischief-maker who walks around with a gun; the youngest, and most strait-laced, is Sam (Abdul Jalloh) who seems immobilised by anxiety. Continue reading...

articles.title: The 37 best Christmas gifts in the UK for tweens – chosen by 10- to 12-year-olds
articles.description: We asked 20 tweenagers what they already own, love and think would make great gifts. Turns out it’s Lego, dance mats and plenty of lotions and potions • The best Christmas gifts for teenagers Buying for someone in the tweenage years can be a balancing act: while some kids are still crafting, enjoying board games and deep into Lego, others have moved on to skincare and guitars. So, in an effort to cover the whole range, I spoke to 20 tweens (from 10 to 12 years old) from across the country. But instead of asking what they want, I quizzed them on the things they already have, truly love and use regularly. Here are their tried and tested gift ideas for a range of prices. Continue reading...

articles.title: How I Christmas Shop with Jamie Oliver: ‘The most important thing? Gravy’
articles.description: Always wondered how celebrities do Christmas, what they wear, eat, and always buy ready-made? The chef and campaigner talks whisky, matching waistcoats and the joy of a local bookshop with the Filter • Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Jamie Oliver is a global chef and campaigner with a 27-year television and publishing career. He is working to improve people’s relationship with food and, through his Ministry of Food, aims to teach more than 1 million people to cook by 2030. Jamie lives in Essex with his wife, Jools, and their children. His latest book, 20 Minute Meals: Real Fast Food , is published by Penguin. *** Continue reading...

articles.title: Are walking pads worth it? We put the best under-desk treadmills to the test
articles.description: Want to get your steps in while working or watching TV? Our expert puts walking pads through their paces to find the best for comfort, noise and ease of storage • The best treadmills for your home You don’t necessarily need to walk 10,000 steps a day to improve your health and wellbeing. In fact, the NHS encourages a slightly more manageable target of just 10 minutes of brisk walking daily to introduce more moderate-intensity physical activity and reduce your risk of early death by up to 15% . However, even squeezing in “brisk walks” can be a chore, with busy schedules and increasingly desk-bound jobs forcing more of us to remain sedentary for long periods. That is where walking pads come in, being lighter, smaller and often easier to store than bulky and tricky-to-manoeuvre running treadmills. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best Christmas things aren’t new – and that’s precisely the point
articles.description: Whether it’s vintage baubles or homemade gifts, there’s joy in a Christmas full of memories and personal touches. Plus, the best coats to keep out the chill this winter • Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here What’s the Christmas decoration you’ve had the longest? Mine is a set of silver paper streamers that originally belonged to my grandparents (and which, if the price in shillings on the original box is anything to go by, pre-date 1971). When I get them out, I can picture my late dad balanced on a chair, pinning them to my childhood dining room ceiling. It’s the old, slightly broken stuff that makes Christmas: the things you bring out every year, imbued with Christmases past. “I love finding a prime spot on the tree for a little beaded fairy I got at a fair in primary school,” says Filter audience editor Ella Jinadu. “It has pipe cleaner arms and legs so you can wrap it around the tree in different poses. When the lights catch the beads, it looks fab.” Jess Cartner-Morley’s November style essentials: fancy flats, sexy knits and a Christmassy pigeon ‘An extravagantly illuminated beast’: the best artificial Christmas trees – tested The best Christmas gifts for

articles.title: The best men’s coats for autumn and winter: 48 favourites for £200 or less
articles.description: From a puffer made of old fishing nets to a trench worthy of Bogart, these are the coats worth braving the cold for • The best men’s shirts for every occasion No one remembers the suit Humphrey Bogart wore at the end of Casablanca, but everyone remembers the trench. The same goes for you this winter: from November to March, your coat is your first impression, so it’s worth getting right. That doesn’t mean you have to spend a fortune: the coats in this list cost £200 or less. The trick to choosing the best coat for you is buying something you’ll still be happy to wear in five years. If you’re feeling unsure, stick to timeless colours – navy, black, camel, brown or moody greens – and shapes that have been around forever: the overcoat, the trench, the car coat or, a more recent classic, the puffer. And when uncertain about fit, always size up – outerwear looks best worn a little loose, and it leaves room for knitwear when freezing January rolls around. Continue reading...

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. There were stiff boxy pleated skirts and tube skirts painted with swirls, and dainty embellished skir

articles.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
articles.description: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. He may wear a lab coat and examine brain regions and neurochemicals, but studying the mechanics, he says, doesn’t damp down the mysteries of consciousness. “For me, actually, I’ve become more spiritual and interest

articles.title: The thermostat wars tearing couples apart: ‘It’s hard to feel sexy when you’re freezing cold’
articles.description: Almost two-thirds of bedfellows disagree about the perfect room temperature – and the issue can affect office workers and housemates too. It oftens lead to subterfuge and skulduggery. So is there any way to reach a truce? Recently I read an item on Threads that made me laugh out loud. “New dating app idea: post your thermostat settings to find your match.” The poster then revealed their own preferences: a balmy 24C by day and a chilly 19C at bedtime. The suggestion elicited a rush of responses. “As someone who married outside their thermostat bracket, all I can say is that this is the most brilliant idea ever,” enthused one user. “Get outta here with that daytime terrarium,” responded another. “Are you storing pallets of produce in your house that you need to keep cold?” chimed in a third. Continue reading...

articles.title: The young women driving the US prenup boom: ‘I want to protect myself’
articles.description: Zillennial couples say they want ‘radical transparency’ around their finances, bucking the idea that prenuptial agreements are rooted in division Kai Amos does not know adult life without her fiance, Garret. They are high school sweethearts who met as teens in Idaho and moved across the country to New York together. They got engaged last year and will be married in September. Their days hum with the constant buzz of wedding planning: picking vendors, writing the guest list, dress shopping. And also meeting with lawyers; the happy couple are working on a prenuptial agreement, to protect their respective assets should they ever get divorced. Amos, who is 30, understands the concept has baggage. Her more conservative friends and family back home in Idaho view prenups as something a rich man (and it is always a man) uses to rein in a woman he suspects of gold digging (and it is always a woman, usually younger). “It was always like the idea of a man trying to take advantage of a woman,” Amos said, “and therefore, it has this negative connection that the man is not going to be a trusted partner.” Continue reading...

articles.title: A moment that changed me: a failed date led to one of the greatest friendships of my life
articles.description: My romance with Steven quickly fizzled, but I had gained something just as good. It made me realise that in the endless, exhausting pursuit of love I had closed myself off to other kinds of connection This autumn is my third anniversary with Steven. In October 2023, we matched on Bumble when I was in his home town of Atlanta for a wedding. We met for dinner downtown and even though we’re from different countries, we discovered a mutual love for the British comedy show Stath Lets Flats. It was a done deal. But Steven isn’t my partner, he’s my friend. And if we’re being teenage about it, I’d probably brand him one of my best, despite living 4,000 miles away. Over the past three years, we’ve visited each other’s homes, holidayed together and met one another’s friends and family. I’ve even had dinner with his ex-wife, whom I also now consider a friend. Steven and I have all the hallmarks of a perfect relationship. We just don’t fancy each other. Continue reading...

articles.title: How a chat with ‘auntie’ helped a young worker bag free money in a UK pensions scheme
articles.description: Joining a company scheme at 18 seemed ‘too expensive’ for Rio until someone close put him right One 20-year-old’s financial future is looking brighter after his aunt convinced him to join his workplace pension and take advantage of the “free money” on offer. Rio started working at 18, too young to be “auto-enrolled” into his company’s pension scheme. He as given the option to join but had decided not to because he felt it was too expensive – but, fortunately for him, his “Auntie Susan” is a pensions expert at a leading retirement firm, and she soon put him right. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why has Royal Mail only delivered letters twice in three months?
articles.description: I am waiting for the overdue results of a cancer test, and the postal service seems to be prioritising parcels over letters In the three months since I moved to my village, I’ve had just two deliveries of letters. One of them was only because I caught a passing postman on a parcel round who arranged one just for me. The bundle contained a bank card, two notifications of an overdue bill I was unaware of, a weeks-old letter from my new water company asking me to set up payments, and a letter about a routine cancer test. There has been nothing since. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Free grand piano’: the scam playing on music lovers’ heartstrings
articles.description: Emails claim to come from a woman whose husband has died – but the offer isn’t what it seems An email pops up in your inbox: a woman whose husband has died is giving away his grand piano for free. She says she would love it to go to someone “who will truly appreciate and care for it”. The piano “is in excellent condition and has brought joy to our home”. The email ends: “If you know of a dedicated student, teacher, family or church that would cherish this piano, please feel free to forward this message to them.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Can AI really save you money on your heating bill? I spent two years testing to find out
articles.description: Samuel Gibbs doubted he could cut costs and still keep warm by putting tech in control. The results surprised him Can smart thermostats and AI reduce your heating bills? Every manufacturer claims the answer is yes , quoting average savings in the 25%, or £180 a year range. But all of these promises are heavily caveated and, with energy costs changing regularly, it can be very difficult to tell what is having an impact. To find out if technology can really help, I spent the last two years comparing my miserly manual control and basic heating schedule to an AI-governed system. The results surprised me. Continue reading...

articles.title: Selena Gomez says vaping has changed her voice. Can e-cigarettes really affect your vocal cords – and is it reversible?
articles.description: Experts say the practice can damage delicate tissues in the voice box and there is not yet sufficient data to say if people can recover Read more in the Antiviral series While vaping is known to cause lung damage, breathlessness and nicotine addiction, the singer and actor Selena Gomez has posted in a video on Instagram that vaping has permanently changed her voice. “Nicotine is so hard to quit and I just wanted to say, if you’re going through it, or if you’re even trying to vape, it’s just not worth it,” she said. “It’s so stupid and it changed my voice. I’m not going to be able to change my voice. I vaped a lot.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Tired all the time? What to know about B12 and if it actually boosts energy levels
articles.description: Med spas are raving about vitamin B12 shots as a pick-me-up. But do they actually make you feel more energized? If you spend time on social media, you may have seen med spa owners and employees describing vitamin B12 shots as a pick-me-up . When they’re run down or facing a busy week, they say, a quick injection gets them through. Some med spas say many people feel an energy lift within a day or two and recommend a shot every few weeks. B12 is essential to your health, and people who don’t get enough of it can feel exhausted or worse. But most people already have plenty of B12, and for them, extra doses aren’t likely to help. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: a lotion to cure autumn dryness – and relieve eczema sufferers’ sore skin
articles.description: Bioderma’s new eczema lotion will be comforting for anyone with dry skin. Plus another brilliant problem solving mosituriser I spent much of my childhood basted in crude, heavy-duty emollient creams and grim bath oils. But few patients are as short-changed as eczema sufferers, whose treatments and regimens are not only joyless, but sometimes provide little reward for the trouble. Although unctuous emollients are necessary to protect a compromised skin barrier, they have a habit of just “sitting” there greasily, refusing to sink in or curtail the itch. The French pharmaceutical brand Bioderma is finally advancing the conversation. Its extensive research into eczema, as well as a recent study of 500 sufferers (about one in five children and one in 10 adults struggle with the condition), were presented as a breakthrough in eczema care at last month’s EADV (European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology) conference in Vienna. Continue reading...

articles.title: Maybe it’s a new tagline. Maybe it’s more punctuation. Maybelline’s 35-year-old slogan has an update
articles.description: First introduced in 1991, ‘Maybe she’s born with it’ is out the door – but is the new slogan a glow-up? Alyx, I hear a certain makeup brand has updated its tagline. Why is this a big deal? The jingle that has been burned into the minds of women around the world since its Christy Turlington-helmed debut in 1991, “Maybe she’s born with it, maybe it’s Maybelline”, has received what has being described as a “modernisation”. In a new campaign with Miley Cyrus, the “she’s” will be replaced with “we’re”, which both changes the observer’s perspective to something a little more self-directed and makes it more inclusive. But it’s a punctuation change that is raising eyebrows. Continue reading...

articles.title: 10 of the best wild winter weekends in the UK
articles.description: Saunas, seal-watching and spectacular skies feature in our picks of great places for a short break to enjoy winter in the raw. Plus boltholes to cosy up in A murmuration of starlings is one of winter’s most mesmerising spectacles; thousands of birds, swooping in formation, before communally roosting to stave off the winter. Piers are a favourite place to roost, with up to 50,000 zooming around in the skies above Aberystwyth, best seen on an afternoon stroll along the prom. The town is also home to the National Library of Wales which is well worth a visit, both for its excellent gift shop and the chance to browse a few of the 8 million books and periodicals within its walls. Y Ffarmers , which is a few miles out of town, is excellent for a long lunch, and Gwesty Cymru , on the seafront, has doubles from £140 B&B. Continue reading...

articles.title: Dream of Birds – documentary
articles.description: What happens when a forest loses its birdsong? Following clues hidden in the sounds birds make while asleep , Argentinian physicist Gabriel Mindlin uncovers a hidden extinction – not of species, but of memory – and sets out to revive vanished melodies before they disappear forever. Part detective story, part cutting-edge science, Mindlin’s mission leads him to the dusty 1960s archives of Buenos Aires naturalist, confirming that some songs no longer echo in the biosphere. So he deploys “robot tutors” to see whether young birds can learn and spread the old songs once again. Read more on this topic: Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs? Continue reading...

articles.title: Private renters in the UK: how difficult is the rental market where you live?
articles.description: We’d like to hear from private renters about rising costs, finding somewhere to live and dealing with landlords Private renters are facing steep rent rises and a shortage of affordable properties, with growing numbers of landlords selling up. The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into force in England in May, introduced new protections for tenants, but many continue to face uncertainty about their housing. While some renters have successfully secured reductions , others are struggling with soaring costs and a highly competitive rental market. Meanwhile England’s housing courts have been overloaded with renters battling evictions . Continue reading...

articles.title: Tell us: did you have a momentous life experience during the solar eclipse?
articles.description: Perhaps you got engaged, married, gave birth, or enjoyed a random act of kindness In August this year, many people stopped to witness the breathtaking solar eclipse. Some peered through colanders to see the rare celestial event or joined friends and family to enjoy this special moment. Continue reading...

Explore all our newsletters: whether you love film, football, fashion or food, we’ve got something for you Continue reading...

articles.description: Get smart, sustainable shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox, every Sunday The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Continue reading...

Sign up any time, and get eight emails direct to your inbox every Sunday morning. Continue reading...

articles.title: Grab the wigs – we’re going to the theatre! We meet the audience superfans going crazy for cosplay
articles.description: Skeleton suits for Phantom of the Opera, garish wigs for Beetlejuice, a Don’t Tell Mama dress for Cabaret … our critic pulls on her cat ears and leotard to investigate a wild new craze It’s an hour before curtain-up and the queue outside the theatre is full of green wigs and blue faces, all amid a sea of black and white stripes. It is Halloween night and these theatregoers of all ages, snaking around a corner of the West End, are in themed dress for the musical Beetlejuice , adapted from the 80s film. In other theatres’ queues you might spot a king from Hamilton, the queens of Six and the wizards of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, all bestowing new meaning to the idea of dressing up for the theatre. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Christmas is all in the preparation!’ Chefs on eight easy things to do now – so you can relax on the big day
articles.description: No one wants to slog away in the kitchen while everyone else gets festive. Thanks to these hacks and recipes from professionals, you won’t have to When it comes to cooking during the festive season, time is tight, fridge space is at a premium and the last thing you want is to be trapped in the kitchen while your family and friends enjoy the fruits of your labour. Luckily, there are plenty of ways to get ahead. “It’s all in the preparation,” says Tom Childs, the head chef at Kerridge’s in London . “Get organised like a commercial kitchen and you’ll be relaxed by the time the big day arrives.” From freezable, deeply delicious gravy to flavoured butters guaranteed to give the driest of meats a juicy kick, from preserves to liven up leftovers to lightweight puddings the whole family can enjoy, I tested the recipes chefs recommend making now to guarantee your Christmas larder is well stocked, no matter who ends up at your dining table. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘You can almost smell the sweat’: striptease artists and steel pans light up this week’s free art shows
articles.description: Four free exhibitions take you from a luxury white enclave in Rio de Janeiro to exhausted erotic dancers touring the US and a culture-changing London address ★★★★☆ Continue reading...

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for torta tenerina, or rich chocolate cake | A kitchen in Rome
articles.description: This soft-but-dense, velvety delight is cake at its most pudding-like. It’s at its prime still warm from the oven, but gets gloriously fudgy after a night in the fridge The note by Elizabeth David is helpful here: “This cake can also be eaten like a pudding” for its soft-dense-velvet-texture. But I am jumping ahead: this week’s column started in Ferrara, a city in the wetlands of the Po delta in the north-eastern corner of Emilia-Romagna. Half medieval lanes and half green avenues and parks, Ferrara is home to one of Europe’s most imposing red-brick castles, one that provides a home to an annual journalism festival run by the magazine Internazionale . Ferrara is also known for a cake. In fact, it was after a discussion about translation and fact-checking with the Italian writer Domenico Starnone and the translator Ann Goldstein that I first ate a wedge of chocolate, butter, egg, sugar and flour torta tenerina. Having just mentioned fact-checking, I am now going to side-step the origin stories. The name, however, more or less translates as “little tender one”, although that “little” refers more to the fact that it is a bit tender, rather than being on the small side. Especially beca

articles.title: Country diary: An ancient bridge, laid low by one storm after another | Sara Hudston
articles.description: Exmoor, Somerset: Tarr Steps is no stranger to flooding, but the damage is becoming more and more frequent Fog cloaked the combe as we walked down to the River Barle, and for the first time in months I wished I were wearing gloves. A red kite wheeled overhead, the dull copper colour of its underparts matching the autumn leaves still clinging to the oaks. Red kites are still fairly uncommon on Exmoor, though their numbers have increased recently as the species pushes west. Several pheasants whirred past, calling loudly in alarm: they are also more numerous now, due to the spread of game-shooting estates. We were heading for Tarr Steps, the longest clapper bridge in Britain, an ancient footbridge nearly 55 metres long, with 17 arches braced across the Barle. It is constructed of pillars of piled rock set about two metres apart, spanned by huge, flat gritstones weighing up to two tonnes each. The whole edifice is held together by bulk and weight, without the aid of mortar, cement or ironwork. Its exact age is uncertain, but the existing structure is considered to be a medieval improvement of a simpler bronze age crossing. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK appoints world’s first special representative for climate security
articles.description: Exclusive: Madeleine Alessandri, former chair of joint intelligence committee, will take on role of advising No 10 on climate-related national security risks The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country. Prime minister Andy Burnham will announce the move on Thursday at Cop31, the UN climate summit, with the new role designed to advise the government on national security risks from the climate crisis before they spell catastrophe. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘A second chance’: children guilty of serious offences will no longer have to declare criminal records
articles.description: Government proposal aims to reduce number of children in custody in England and Wales and boost youth employment Children found guilty of robbery, dealing drugs to other children or violent disorder will no longer have to disclose their criminal records to prospective employers under sweeping government proposals to change the youth justice system. People in England and Wales will not have to share records of crimes committed when they were under 18 for the rest of their lives under the proposals, which ministers say will boost youth employment and make life fairer for people from disadvantaged backgrounds in particular. Continue reading...

articles.title: Some young disabled people to lose Pip in Milburn plan – but can apply to local fund
articles.description: Exclusive: Former health secretary wants to ‘tear up the old approach’, and end ongoing payments to certain under-25s Some young people with disabilities will lose their personal independence payments but will be able to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment, Alan Milburn’s review will recommend. While those with the most severe needs’ entitlement will be protected, others will be asked to apply for money for specific purposes rather than an ongoing payment. Continue reading...

articles.title: Two men found guilty of helping Iran try to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists
articles.description: Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on targets Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services. Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31: how far off target are we? - video
articles.description: As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are meeting in Turkey for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. Madeleine Finlay tells co-host Ian Sample why these negotiations are so critical and what the chances are of meaningful change. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
articles.description: Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit. Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals. Continue reading...

articles.title: National security of all countries at risk due to climate crisis, UK foreign secretary warns
articles.description: Exclusive: Ed Miliband says sci-fi scenarios of destruction ‘now regular occurrences’, as he prepares to address Cop31 The national security of all countries is at risk from the climate crisis, as “science fiction” scenarios of widespread destruction are already coming true and economic shocks from fossil fuels are now the norm rather than the exception, the UK’s foreign secretary is to warn world leaders gathered in Turkey. Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Goats are good. They listen’: the herder who defeated Montenegro’s military – and can identify her cows’ herby burps
articles.description: To Hold a Mountain tells the incredible story of a woman whose way of life was threatened when she heard her pastures were set to become a Nato training zone The star of To Hold a Mountain is having trouble with her goats, which keep escaping. So my interview with Mileva “Gara” Jovanović is rescheduled to a moment where the animals are under control and Gara can descend from the peaks to her small winter residence in a small village near the capital of Podgorica, for a video call. “You have to take care of them because they are always searching for their paths,” says Gara, whose Montenegrin is translated into English by Biljana Tutorov, the joint writer-director of the stunning film about Gara’s life in the mountains of Sinjajevina. “But the goats are good, especially when they know the shepherdess. I’m a good shepherdess. They listen to me.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Obesity: how to stop millions being misdiagnosed - video
articles.description: An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat. Guardian Science editor Ian Sample takes co-host Madeleine Finlay through why BMI is flawed, and how the new framework could improve precision medicine. Continue reading...

articles.title: Women came forward to protect others. They’re heroes | Lucy Beaumont
articles.description: So many have contacted me about their experiences. Women used to be blamed for what men did to them, but I can feel things changing Lucy Beaumont is a comedian and author At the forefront of everything going on recently are young women and girls. They were vulnerable because of their age or their class, and also because of power dynamics. These women and girls went through something traumatising, all of them. As did all of the women and girls who I’m sure are coming forward now. Everyone knows there are other men who traumatised girls they’ve worked with, while being paid very, very large amounts of money. Lucy Beaumont is a comedian and author Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: Look at the Poundland scandal and see a crisis that goes beyond Britain’s high streets | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: ‘I look out for my team,’ a store manager tells me, but Poundland’s US owner doesn’t care. Labour may be too late to prevent it becoming yet another casualty of venture capital In the Poundland I visit, a treasure trove of bargains, the staff are dejected. The shelves are emptying because the owners have withheld £50m needed for new stock and paying wages. It’s just one of 600 stores in peril, and these employees just a few of 12,000 at risk of losing their jobs – with 30,000 jobs at risk in supply chains. On Tuesday £10m was released : not enough, but preventing instant collapse. Gordon Brothers, the US owner that bought Poundland for a symbolic £1 last year, specialises in buying and “restructuring” distressed companies. Under pressure, it extended the deadline by 10 working days before putting this profitable business into administration. It profits more by closing Poundland down and breaking it up. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: UK car industry to press EU for two-year delay to Brexit EV tariffs
articles.description: ‘Rules of origin’ on vehicle batteries due to come into force on 1 January if deal on new delay is not reached The UK car industry is preparing to push for a two-year delay to Brexit tariffs on electric cars traded with the EU, after an initial European proposal suggested a shorter delay. Tariffs are due to kick in on 1 January for the majority of electric cars traded between the EU and UK unless the two sides can come to an agreement to delay for a second time the implementation of “rules of origin” on batteries. Continue reading...

articles.title: Poundland owner secures two extra weeks to ensure retail chain’s survival
articles.description: US investment firm Gordon Brothers is ‘taking due care’ to consider if one of three bidders has enough funds Poundland’s owner has said it is “taking due care” to consider if one of three bidders had enough funds to ensure its survival after the troubled budget retail chain secured two more weeks to find a deal. The management of Poundland , which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors on Thursday morning. articles.title: Burberry returns to profit as sales soar, from £85 socks to £9,000 coats
articles.description: CEO says ‘democratic approach’ has helped brand outperform tough market, with big rises in China and US Burberry has returned to profit as its back-to-basics strategy drove strong sales of the British brand’s coats, jackets and handbags over the summer. Joshua Schulman, the chief executive, said the luxury brand had outperformed a “challenging luxury market” to achieve sales growth of 6%, helped by strong online and wholesale sales particularly in China and the US. “Our strategy is working,” he said. articles.title: Adam and Joe on spoofing ‘Christopher No-Laughs’ with a toys’ Odyssey – and Patrick Stewart’s haunted house
articles.description: Adam Buxton and Joe Cornish returned for a night on stage as packed with pop-culture pisstakes as the show that made them a 90s TV cult. Here’s what we learned ‘Warning: The Adam and Joe Show is a high-density programme.” In the late 90s, that was your Friday-night cue to press record on the video player for Adam Buxton and Joe Cornish’s pop-culture potpourri of sketches, pranks and lovingly crafted, lo-fi movie parodies featuring figurines and cuddly toys. Thirty years after its debut, the duo – now both 57 – recreated their old den in the improbable environs of the Royal Albert Hall for a three-hour anniversary show as packed as the rapid-fire series. Here’s a select few things we learned from an evening of clips, chat and ridiculously catchy songs … Continue reading...

articles.title: Blackhaine: Saints in the Wethouse review | Alexis Petridis's album of the week
articles.description: (XL Recordings) His Playboi Carti collabs may have dragged Tom Heyes out of the underground, but this bracing debut remains far from the mainstream, full of garbled barks and walls of noise On the second track on his debut album, Tom Heyes accuses lesser artists of copying him. “What the fuck you even take me for?” he barks on Northside Needs Me , over a grinding, distorted bassline that comes punctuated with stammering, rave-y vocal samples. “Too much noise shit, replicating what I played before.” Of course, charging that others are merely imitating what you did previously is a venerable rap tradition: the track that gave said practice its longstanding name, Bite’n My Stylee by Original Concept, is now 40 years old. Perhaps it’s true that others have been copying the approach that Heyes has minted under the alias of Blackhaine, but if so, it seems faintly remarkable, because his approach is so determinedly unique. Continue reading...

articles.title: Public Access Afterworld by Jane Schoenbrun review – horror in the TV static
articles.description: The Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma writer-director’s first novel is a wry, hugely fun journey into the dark world behind our screens Public Access Afterworld is the first novel by Jane Schoenbrun, director of cult-hit horror film I Saw the TV Glow and the more recent Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma; movies in which screens are a permeable barrier and people are menaced by the uncanny realms that lurk behind them. Here the main character is Bethany Peters, a young trans woman working as a content moderator at a YouTube-like company called GlobalVill. Her job is to watch “offensive, illegal, disturbing videos that have no place on the internet” and press a red button to remove those that violate the code of conduct. One night she sees a video posted by someone with the username JulesPublicAccessAfterworld, a visibly malnourished non-binary kid who reminds Bethany of herself “before her stay in hospital, and everything that happened to her there”. The kid says to camera, “If you’re watching this, David Sawyer, this is for you,” then takes out a razor blade and draws it down their arm. Soon Bethany is off on a quest to save them, in the course of which she will learn that sh

articles.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
articles.description: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave , Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country , except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue reading...

articles.title: Punks, sex workers and society in transition: documenting postwar Japan – in pictures
articles.description: A Long Shadow: Postwar Japan Through the Lens will be the first show of Japanese photography in more than three decades at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. The exhibit brings together 15 intergenerational artists as well as photographic prints, including more than 25 books and magazines and a video installation, all combining to show how photographers in Japan documented the country in the decades after the second world war. The exhibition runs until 2 May 2027 Continue reading...

articles.title: School-night wine - the best bottles for an impromptu midweek treat
articles.description: Five wines that hit the spot without breaking the bank Last week, I made The One Sauce from the new Ottolenghi book, Simple Too , and it might well be the zenith of tomato sauces. We ate this gloriously garlicky, vinegar-spiked number with pasta, and it was a revelation. After one bite, it felt rude not to have some wine with it and, before I knew it, I had a glass of red in front of me. Today, I am championing school-night wine. Not because I want to be a bad influence, but because, in this restrained, over-scheduled, all-or-nothing age, we risk losing the impromptu pleasure of a nice drop – with food, say, or with a friend who has popped by, or just to offset the nervous strain of the children’s bedtime. Occasionally, “It’s a school night” is reason enough to do something. Continue reading...

articles.title: My best friend is pregnant. I’m happy for her but not good with babies. How can I be supportive? | Leading questions
articles.description: Children vary just like the rest of us, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith . You don’t know you’re bad with this baby yet, because you don’t know them yet Read more Leading questions My best friend is having her first child. I don’t know how to respond without coming off as a total jerk if she ever asks me and my fiance to babysit . What can I do to still be a supportive friend and how do I clear the air on the matter? Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘A web of canals and cobbled streets’: a city break in Haarlem in the Netherlands
articles.description: A short ride from Amsterdam, this laid-back city has great museums, cosy bars and a new exhibition featuring the works of Rembrandt and local artist Frans Hals this winter It’s only 15 minutes away from the Dutch capital by train, but Haarlem feels a million miles from Amsterdam, and perhaps provides a more typical glimpse of the Netherlands than trailing around the well-worn tourist trail of Van Gogh, coffee shops and red lights. An attractive city of cobbled streets, gabled houses and canals, Haarlem is, as the Dutch would say, a gezellig sort of place – cosy, convivial, and full of intriguing nooks and corners. I’ve been coming here for years, and it seems odd that Haarlem is not better known, at least to UK visitors. This winter there’s the added draw of an exhibition devoted to the works of a local boy, the 17th-century painter Frans Hals, and his better-known contemporary Rembrandt in the city’s Frans Hals Museum (until 28 February 2027). No one really knows whether these two titans of the Dutch Golden Age of the 16th and 17th centuries ever met, but seeing their work hung together like this is powerful and compelling. articles.title: Tell us: did you move to the countryside for retirement and come to regret it?
articles.description: As England’s chief medical officer warns of the challenges of growing older in rural areas, we’d like to hear from people who have struggled with isolation or accessing services and support England’s chief medical officer Chris Whitty has warned of the potential downsides of choosing to spend the later part of your life in a rural area. He urged people to think carefully about the challenges of rural life as they get older, including poor access to healthcare, limited public transport and the risk of becoming isolated or dependent on others. We want to hear from the people people who have experienced these challenges. Did you move to the countryside for your retirement and find it more difficult to access the services and support you need? Are you feeling dependent on others to get around and access amenities, leaving you wishing you’d stayed in a town or city? Or have you moved back to a city, finding rural life too isolating as you become older? Continue reading...

articles.title: Cunk on Cinema review – Diane Morgan baffles Hollywood with some of the stupidest jokes ever told
articles.description: This sensationally idiotic guide to film history is hilarious. From a crude Mary Poppins gag to confusing the hell out of Michael Bay, I could listen to Cunk’s surreal tosh all day In a world of slow-burn, jargon-littered dramas, there’s something to be said for the TV programme that sets out its stall within the first 12 seconds. Cunk on Cinema is one such programme. The latest series from Diane Morgan’s sensationally idiotic documentarian is a three-part history of film that begins with our host reeling off some of humanity’s greatest achievements in her deadpan Bolton tones. Specifically, “conquering the landscape, growing the great wall of Chinese, discovering Mona Lisa and inventing global warming”. If you think that list is funny, you’ll enjoy what is essentially a vehicle for some of the stupidest jokes ever written. If you find that kind of malapropism and misapprehension childish, I suggest you switch off immediately. We first encountered Philomena Cunk in 2012 as a spoof talking head on Charlie Brooker’s annual end-of-year Screenwipe special. articles.title: The Good Daughter review – the best thing about this legal thriller? Brendan Gleeson’s sad toilet fart
articles.description: For a drama that is meant to explore female trauma, Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy are given very little to do as small-town lawyers. It is Gleeson who steals the show as their broken father who earns the name Shatticus Finch “Why is ma laaahf filled with contrary feee-males ?” grumbles dilapidated defence lawyer Rusty Quinn (Brendan Gleeson), his deep south vowels stretching like grilled cheese across his cluttered desk. Poor Rusty. As the father of two headstrong lawyer daughters, this sunken beanbag of fading masculinity is forced daily to endure the contrariness of feee-males who are forever challengin’ the status quo. “This is all bullshit,” snaps elder daughter Sam (Rose Byrne), by way of illustration. “You’re a dipshit,” adds Charlie (Meghann Fahy), thoughtfully. They sure don’t make his laaahf easy! But the sisters love ol’ Rusty, or at least do their best to tolerate his excruciating aphorisms (“Never kick a fresh turd on a hot day,” etc), and when a school shooting forces them to confront a long-buried family tragedy, the Quinns pull together. They need each other. Dammit, the whole town needs them. After all, shouts Charlie, “We’re the only lawyers that don’t roll over for

articles.title: The Guardian view on Gaza’s misery: don’t let Palestinian deaths mount in this bleak winter | Editorial
articles.description: The formation of a new Israeli government won’t stop the killing, but sustained international pressure must be applied What do you call a ceasefire when the firing has not ceased? The killings in Gaza decreased when the truce was announced last October, but they did not end. Israel’s strike on Thursday morning on one of the few remaining functioning hospitals , which killed six people and wounded 28 more, was the first on a healthcare facility since then. But it was not an anomaly. About four Palestinians a day have died on average since the ceasefire was declared. The Israeli military said that it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters in the attack on Nasser hospital, without providing evidence. Its record does not inspire confidence in the accuracy of its account. Multiple UN experts and health campaigners have warned of the deliberate targeting of medical facilities and healthcare workers. Israeli military personnel have also described the shockingly high level of civilian deaths tolerated as “collateral damage” in targeting even low-level fighters after the brutal Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial
articles.description: Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs Britain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry. The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task . Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech. Continue reading...

articles.title: We need to rethink climate action away from the Cop talks | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to an article by Fiona Harvey in which she questioned whether progress is being made 10 years on from the Paris treaty As world leaders gathered in Turkey for the UN climate talks, Fiona Harvey was right to ask, “What’s the point?” ( What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?, 7 November ). She pointed to how over 10 years ago in Paris, countries came together for the 21st conference and signed an agreement that aimed to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. For the past two years, temperatures “have exceeded that threshold”. I was at last year’s climate summit in Brazil, where it was obvious that the Cop process itself is a big part of the problem. The agreed text did not include “fossil fuels”, not to mention any reference to transition away from them. This is largely the result of how negotiations are conducted, as they rely on unanimous consent by all participating countries. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why parliament needs to move out – and move on | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to Simon Jenkins’s article suggesting that parliament should relocate out of London Simon Jenkins is right to characterise parliament as “outdated and immune to reform” ( Notre-Dame was restored in five years and under budget. But the Palace of Westminster? No chance, 6 November ). However, it is not only cost, practicality and design that are compelling reasons to empty the building and move to purpose-built premises. The building and the institution in their present form are entirely inappropriate for the workplace of a modern democracy. The self-entitlement evident in the resistance to moving out, such as that voiced by, among others, Jacob Rees-Mogg, illustrates the assumptions of class and leadership roles in those most comfortable with the status quo, and with the arcane, outdated building and rituals, which must seem bizarre and intimidating to anyone not raised in privilege and the traditional public schools. Continue reading...

articles.title: Clem Cattini: remember he was a Womble – and almost a member of Led Zeppelin | Letters
articles.description: Clem Cattini, who played on more than 40 No 1 hits as a session musician, was very modest about his talent, writes Mark Sweet . Plus a letter from DLL Gould Working as a propman on Blue Peter in 1998, I was privileged to witness a performance of Remember You’re a Womble by the furry pop band as they prepared for a nationwide tour. During a break in rehearsals I chatted to a heavily sweating Bungo on the drum kit. “By the way,” I asked him, “what do you do when you’re not being a Womble?” Continue reading...

articles.title: Participating in art and culture has measurable benefits on our wellbeing | Letter
articles.description: William Rees says Ealing council’s workshops have shown that even an hour spent on a creative pursuit can change someone’s day Reading Emma Brockes’ response to a recent Art Fund study, I felt the significance of the research may have been lost in its packaging ( Art is good for your health? articles.title: Ebenezer review – Johnny Depp’s Scrooge tries to exorcise ghosts of business past
articles.description: The latest film version of the Dickens classic A Christmas Carol is decent enough, though its star is rather better as the legendary miser before redemption arrives Here for lovers of Dickens – and fans of subtext – is an unexpectedly watchable new movie version of A Christmas Carol starring a top-hatted and heavily madeup Johnny Depp; it is a film about whether it’s possible for a man to earn redemption before it is too late. (The answer is … sure, as long as you say sorry and change your ways. But Mr Scrooge never launched a libel action against the Sun for calling him an un-Christmassy old meanie.) In fact, screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern and director Ti West have put together a perfectly serviceable, faithful adaptation – a tradaptation, if you will – of Dickens’s masterpiece about the hideous old miser saved from damnation on Christmas Eve by the appearance of three Christmas ghosts, from yuletides past, present and future. It sticks to the accepted narrative beats and more or less all the familiar episodes, but with a few twists. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tommy Walsh obituary
articles.description: Burly TV presenter who brought his building knowledge and power tools to the BBC’s gardening makeover show Ground Force Tommy Walsh, who has died aged 69, brought decking and pergolas, as well as rippling muscles and a brusque manner, to the BBC gardening show Ground Force, alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock. The trio transformed gardens for members of the public in just two days, and the programme (which ran from 1997 until 2005) made the burly 6ft 5in Walsh a star after years running his own building and landscaping business. “People want textures, shapes and surfaces in the garden that you wouldn’t get from planting alone,” he said. Armed with a power drill, sledgehammer and a host of other tools, he did the back-breaking landscaping work before Titchmarsh, the gardener and broadcaster, and Charlie Dimmock, a garden centre worker, moved in to do the planting. Homeowners would go away and return to find the results of the surprise makeover, organised clandestinely by family members or friends; many were delighted, some less so. Continue reading...

articles.title: The planet ‘is being killed’, Greta Thunberg tells Cop31 climate summit

Thunberg , 23, the Swedish activist who became famous for heading the school climate strike movement, delivered her stark message to those gathered at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, amid the ongoing failure by countries to adequately address the climate crisis. articles.title: ‘Women are pitted against each other. It’s a bloodsport’: Billie Piper on industry infighting, Elsinore’s Oscar buzz and thriving on personal crisis

articles.title: Experience: I was disembowelled by a hippo on my honeymoon
articles.description: A mother hippopotamus protecting her young is one of the most fearsome forces of nature. Luckily, I’d just married someone ready to meet it head-on Anna and I got married in Portugal in September last year. We had been together for 13 years. She said in her vows, “I don’t know what life is going to have in store for us, but I know our love for each other is always constant.” Ten days later, I found myself in a swamp in Botswana with my intestines hanging out of my back. articles.title: More than 60% of Germany’s female soldiers report harassment or abuse

The first comprehensive study of its kind into the Bundeswehr, conducted by the Centre for Military History and Social Sciences in Potsdam and released this week, comes as the military is trying to attract new recruits in response to global threats. articles.title: Boxer on death row in Iran vows ‘not to bow before oppression’ after winning rights prize
articles.description: Political prisoner Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran, given prestigious Magnitsky humanitarian award A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”. Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani , an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran . articles.title: World is now in ‘age of electricity’, energy agency chief says
articles.description: Exclusive: Fossil fuels no longer dominant energy source, IEA leader says, as summit considers electrification pledge The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said. Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘They’ve cut all entry-level jobs’: unlikely seaside town on frontline of AI threat
articles.description: Bournemouth became a hub for thousands of finance jobs after the 1980s big bang, but new tech risks hurting Dorset’s economy A few minutes’ drive from Bournemouth’s sandy beachfront, on the site of a former farm, lies an unlikely nerve centre of international finance. Here, miles from the glass towers of London’s Canary Wharf, more than 5,300 staff including compliance officers, analysts and software engineers help process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day for the largest US bank, JP Morgan. The sprawling five-hectare (13-acre) campus, which hosted just 650 workers when it opened in 1986, has solidified Dorset’s status as one of Britain’s largest financial hubs outside London. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I spend less, that’s all that matters’: life in the world’s most electrified countries
articles.description: Owning an electric car, driving an electric motorbike taxi, riding scooters – we speak to people in Oslo, Kigali and Shanghai about their everyday routines The race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s UN climate summit: increasing the use of electricity – particularly from clean sources – has the potential to improve daily life for people around the world. The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The global figure currently stands at 23%, but some countries are already striding ahead. As 100,000 delegates, negotiators and world leaders thrash out the details in Antalya, Turkey , the Guardian spoke to three people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out what life looks like in more highly electrified countries. Continue reading...

articles.title: Did Indonesia’s vice-president just resign because he didn’t have a high school diploma?

articles.title: 12 12 12 review – Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s super fun heist hunt
articles.description: From the moment a contortionist crawls out of a bank vault, the 12-hour hunt for the culprits is a thrilling ride. Just suspend your disbelief a bit and strap in for a fantastic time A contortionist crawls out of a safety deposit box in the wall of an underground Swiss bank vault, legs wrapped around his waist, feet resting on his lumbar spine, landing on hands and displaced knees on the tiled floor. You know what? SOLD. You have just earned my undivided attention for the next hour of whatever you want to present to me. Under such highly promising circumstances does the new heist thriller 12 12 12 begin. It stars Anthony Mackie of the Marvel Cinematic Universe and Jamie Dornan (building a nice career since 2013’s The Fall , if we gloss over the 50 Shades movies and the one where he played a romantic hero who believed he was a bee ) as its antagonists locked in an international cat-and-mouse game over eight episodes. articles.title: ‘The time is ripe’: ex-helicopter engineer poised to be Germany’s first female president
articles.description: Backed by MPs from across the political divide, Bavarian Ilse Aigner offers an approachability and warmth the chancellor lacks Germany has had 12 presidents since the end of the second world war, all of them men. Now, for the first time, the federal republic is on the brink of getting a female head of state. But Ilse Aigner, the lead candidate for the post, is unusual in more ways than one. “No law degree. No marriage. No penis,” is how the left-leaning Taz newspaper put it this week – a wry, if blunt, assessment of what a break with history the 61-year-old Bavarian represents. Continue reading...

articles.title: Hamlet Hail to the Thief could have been rotten but redeems Radiohead’s ‘record that got away’ | Alexis Petridis
articles.description: The band’s uneven 2003 album has been judiciously reworked to accompany a staging of Shakespeare’s tragedy with quite extraordinary results According to the programme notes, Thom Yorke had serious reservations about director Christine Jones’ idea to stage a production of Hamlet featuring music from Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief. Who can blame him? Many criticisms have been laid at Radiohead’s door but being hopelessly naff isn’t one of them, and, alas, naff is very much the adjective you’d apply to a lot of attempts to meld Shakespeare and rock music. You’re often in the realm of high camp – portentous, Bard-quoting heavy metal lyrics; Return to the Forbidden Planet ’s jokey blending of The Tempest with 50s rock’n’roll; 2015’s These Paper Bullets , which relocated Much Ado About Nothing to swinging London, complete with Beatle-y songs by Green Day’s Billie Joe Armstrong – or of buttock-clenching disasters like Catch My Soul, a 1971 rock adaptation of Othello which required Black American soul singer PP Arnold to star opposite impresario Jack Good, playing the title role in blackface. Continue reading...

articles.title: Progressives are still so pessimistic, but why? The populist right can and will be defeated | Andy Beckett
articles.description: From the US midterms to Brazil and Hungary, extremists are floundering yet the left still overestimates their power. Reality is on our side From Brazil to Hungary and Britain to the US, why are so many people so surprised by the right’s election defeats? Flávio Bolsonaro, Viktor Orbán, Reform UK, the Tories and a vast array of Republican candidates have all been rejected in national or local contests this year, even in usually reliably conservative Mississippi. Apparently impregnable incumbents and populist insurgents alike have been beaten, often by big margins . The supposedly ascendant global right has been out-organised, out-thought, outmanoeuvred and outnumbered. Yet each time this happens – which is more often than the usual gloomy narrative of our politics allows – many liberals and leftists absorb and share the good news almost with wonderment . Rightwing governments such as Donald Trump’s may have been struggling for many months, having made countless impossible or incompatible promises and strategic blunders, and opinion polls may have been consistently pointing towards a meltdown, but their actual election defeats are seen as miracles: unexpected moments of joy in the mo

articles.title: As housing protests sweep Portugal, police and politicians here seem bent on making the crisis worse | Ana Naomi de Sousa
articles.description: While Spain, Germany and the UK have all introduced laws protecting renters’ rights, Luís Montenegro’s centre-right government is empowering landlords As Storm Charles reached Portugal’s shores this week, flights were aborted, schools were closed, and the global Web Summit in Lisbon was forced to cancel a whole day of lucrative events. But even the promise of some very bad weather was not enough to deter housing protesters from setting up camp for another night on the streets. Since 14 October, echoing recent eruptions over housing in Spain, and the fierce student-led protests in France , Lisbon and Porto have become the focus for encampments and daily protests drawing people in their thousands. articles.title: ‘It was a train wreck! I was terrified’: how the new James Bond will be announced – and what can go wrong
articles.description: As Amazon MGM Studios prepares to announce the next 007, much rides on how the news is broken. From double bookings to health and safety embarrassments, we look back at how not to do it And then there were five. While nothing has been officially announced, it is widely understood that the shortlist to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond is now down to a handful of actors: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult. The hunt for a new Bond comes at a propitious moment for the franchise as a whole, 25 films in (not counting the two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983). After Daniel Craig stood down from the role after completing No Time to Die (in which Bond appeared to be killed in a missile strike), Amazon MGM Studios paid over $1bn to acquire “creative control” from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, the British-American heirs to the series’ original producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films. articles.title: The sinister power of Friday 13th: how this maligned date affects our lives
articles.description: Property sales that complete on this day have a lower median price. Air fares are cheaper. Weddings are non-existent. And motor collisions increase. How did it become so mired in superstition? “I have only worked one Friday 13th wedding in my 14 years in business,” says Caroline Smyth, a photographer and celebrant based in Larne, Northern Ireland. “I definitely think it is down to the fact that it’s a date surrounded by superstition. People are maybe afraid it’s a bad omen for their marriage.” Smyth’s sole Friday 13th wedding, in September 2013, was the first she ever photographed – and it kickstarted her career. But for many businesses, the date is not so auspicious. From weddings to flights, job interviews to elective surgeries, many people avoid booking anything of significance on this date, believing it to be bad luck. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve | Simon Jenkins
articles.description: For all the supposed improvements, inspectors still obsess over statistics and adjectives, but surely school success depends on teachers and parents The government regulation of state schools by Ofsted in England is a fiasco. Following the 2023 suicide of the Reading headteacher Ruth Perry, after her school was downgraded from outstanding to inadequate, Ofsted appears to have referred to a dictionary. Single words were replaced by colour-coded report cards , which use a wider range of different adjectives to grade abstractions such as personal development and wellbeing, achievement and leadership. Never has the concept of “education” seemed so empty. The reaction of the teaching profession to the new code has itself been devastating, as highlighted in a recent survey that showed more than half of headteachers in England polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are now considering early retirement as a result of the experience. This sense of misery was also illustrated in a poll conducted by the National Education Union one year on from the introduction of the new framework, with 65% saying it is the same as or worse than before. Simon Jenkins is a Guardia

articles.title: Digested week: Do we really have to see Liz Truss at the Cenotaph for the next 30 years? | John Crace
articles.description: At some point even Liz won’t remember why she’s there. Meanwhile, Nige wants more air time, and Boris Johnson couldn’t have made less effort Like most people, I assume, I had always thought the Remembrance Sunday service at the Cenotaph was a time to think of those who died in the two world wars and later armed conflicts. It turns out that Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform, sees it differently. I was listening to Dicky being interviewed on the Jeremy Kyle show on TalkTV – Yes, I know, I’ve only myself to blame – when suddenly he went into a tirade on the BBC’s coverage of the service. His principal complaint was that Nigel Farage had not been given enough air time, though he later morphed into a rant about antisemitism. I never did quite work out how the two were meant to be linked. I’m sure the BBC will reflect seriously on this lapse of judgment in its debrief of the programme and will next year have several cameras trained on Nige throughout the service. articles.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
articles.description: Football and the art world have long remained distant but the breadth of entries for this year’s award revivals a healthy revival It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player . You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball. These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Association launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, with its crowds flocking to Bolton Wanderers’ then home ground, Burnden Park. An exhibition of the submissions, Football and The Fine Arts, toured the country and the FA secretary, Sir Stanley Rous, said he hoped it would finally break
